items.title: dotdash
items.text:
dotdash gets devices in a censored network out to the open internet through a server of yours abroad. It comes as four morzer bundles, released together from one tag:

Bundle Runs on What it does dotdash a server abroad Xray REALITY on 443 in front of a cover site; everything leaves through your upstream proxy dotdash-relay a machine inside the country carries phones, clients and canaries on to the server while only domestic addresses get through dotdash-client a Linux machine on the client side a proxy port, the whole machine, or a whole LAN through dotdash dotdash-canary a machine inside the country connects as a device would, and alerts when it can't get through

Start with the server: its tasks print the other three's setup. The client and the canary reach it as phones do, directly or through a relay.

items.title: What every machine needs
items.text:
Docker ≥ 28 with Compose ≥ 2.35, sops, age, and morzer ≥ 0.15.0. On a fresh Debian or Ubuntu machine, bootstrap.sh installs them, turns on security updates, and sets SSH to keys only:

curl -fsSLO https://morzecrew.github.io/dotdash/bootstrap.sh
less bootstrap.sh && sudo bash bootstrap.sh

Installing morzer by hand: install.sh --dir /usr/local/bin. sudo and morzer's timers don't look in ~/.local/bin.

Every bundle ships the key it is signed with: morzer init prints it, trusts it, and requires every later release to be signed by it.

items.title: Releases
items.text:
Tag ghcr.io/morzecrew/<bundle>:stable the newest release (vX.Y.Z tags), release key ghcr.io/morzecrew/<bundle>:X.Y.Z one release ghcr.io/morzecrew/<bundle>:main every push to main, dev key; may be broken

<bundle> is dotdash, dotdash-relay, dotdash-client or dotdash-canary. These docs are versioned with the releases: the version menu shows each released minor, and dev follows main.

items.title: Canary
items.text: The dotdash-canary bundle (ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-canary) runs on a machine inside the network you worry about. It connects to a dotdash server, or a relay, as a device would, and fails doctor when it can't get through: you hear about a block before your users do. It needs Docker, sops, age and morzer (bootstrap.sh), and no open port.

items.title: Install
items.text:
1. On the server, add a <uuid> canary line to vless_clients, then print the canary's setup:

    sudo EDITOR=nano morzer secret edit vless_clients
sudo morzer task run canary-config --output -- canary

  2. On the canary machine, run what that printed: init, four secrets, apply. The recovery recipient can be the server's own.

  3. Alerts: add a notify target and run doctor every 10 minutes:

    sudo morzer notify target add https://hooks.example/morzer
sudo morzer config set doctor.schedule='*:0/10'

items.title: What it checks
items.text:
By default the canary checks REALITY on 443. Profiles add a transport:

init flag Also checks --profile xhttp XHTTP, through the server's cover site --profile xhttp-reality XHTTP with REALITY, on its own port

Each check fetches probe_url through dotdash, in up to three tries.

To measure rather than check, measure runs each transport a number of times and prints the success rate, timeouts and latency as JSON:

sudo morzer task run measure --output -- 50

items.title: Several servers, and relays
items.text: A canary watches one server. With several servers, canary-config prints how to point a canary at each of the others. To watch a relay instead, run the commands its relay-entry prints on the canary, without the xhttp profiles: the canary then connects through the relay, as a phone on that network would.

items.title: Reference
items.text: Parameter Default server none, given at init the server's domain, sent as the TLS server name; a relay's site address none, given at init where to connect: normally the same domain; an IP, a CDN's name, or a relay's address port 443 the server's https_port xhttp_reality_port 8443 the server's xhttp_reality_port reality_public_key none, given at init the REALITY public key, the pbk of a link probe_url https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204 what each check fetches through dotdash; any 2xx is healthy Secret vless_id the canary's id, its line in the server's vless_clients vless_encryption the encryption= value of a link reality_short_id the sid= value of a REALITY link xhttp_path the path= value of an XHTTP link, without the leading %2F Task measure --output -- [count] [url] [timeout] each transport count times (20 by default), as JSON

items.title: Client
items.text:
The dotdash-client bundle (ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-client) runs on a Linux machine on the client side: a home server, a Raspberry Pi, an office VM. It runs mihomo from one device's subscription URL and sends traffic through dotdash, over whichever of that device's links answers fastest.

Three ways in, from least to most:

What goes through dotdash Set up Proxy port apps set to use a SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy, on this machine or, shared, on the LAN the default Whole machine every connection on this machine, its containers' too, with no proxy settings the tun profile LAN gateway every device whose gateway is this machine tun with gateway=true

Rules send chosen destinations around dotdash or refuse them; everything else goes through it. With dotdash out of reach, nothing leaves around it.

items.title: Install
items.text:
The machine needs Docker, sops, age and morzer (bootstrap.sh).

  1. On the server, with subscriptions on, add a device for this machine, a <uuid> home line in vless_clients, and print its URL:

    sudo EDITOR=nano morzer secret edit vless_clients
sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- home

  2. On the client machine:

    morzer secret recipients generate-recovery-key ~/client-recovery.key   # keep it off the machine
sudo morzer init --release oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-client:stable \
  --recovery-recipient age1…
sudo morzer secret set subscription_url    # the URL from step 1
sudo morzer apply

  3. Check that the port gets out through dotdash; 204 means it does:

    curl --proxy socks5h://127.0.0.1:7890 https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204 -w '%{http_code}\n'

The port is on 127.0.0.1, for this machine alone. Next: share it with the LAN, or send the whole machine through dotdash.

items.title: The subscription
items.text: mihomo fetches the subscription every subscription_interval seconds (an hour), through dotdash, so it stays current where only dotdash gets through, such as through a relay while only domestic addresses do. When that fails, as on a first start, it fetches directly. It keeps the last copy, so a restart while the URL is out of reach starts on the links it fetched last. Relays in the subscription are links like the others: while only a relay gets through, the client goes through it.

items.title: Share the proxy port
items.text:
The proxy port, 7890, is SOCKS5 and HTTP on one port. At first it listens on 127.0.0.1, for this machine alone, and asks for nothing. To let other devices on the LAN use it, publish it on an address they can reach. Devices then have to give a username and a password: dotdash and the generated proxy_password secret.

Note

192.168.1.10 below stands for this machine's LAN address: use yours.

  1. Find this machine's LAN address, the one devices reach it at:

    hostname -I     # this machine's addresses, such as 192.168.1.10

  2. Publish the port on that address:

    sudo morzer config set listen=192.168.1.10

    Or on every address of this machine with listen=0.0.0.0, which keeps working if the address changes but also publishes the port on any other network the machine is on. Allow 7890/tcp from the LAN if the machine has a firewall.

  3. Print the settings devices need:

    sudo morzer task run proxy-config --output

    For devices on the network (as secret as a password):
socks5h://dotdash:<password>@192.168.1.10:7890
http://dotdash:<password>@192.168.1.10:7890

Or, for an app that asks for them apart: server 192.168.1.10, port 7890,
username dotdash, password <password>.

    With listen=0.0.0.0 the task can't tell which address devices use, so give it after --: proxy-config --output -- 192.168.1.10.

A new password, which every device then needs:

sudo morzer secret rotate proxy_password
sudo morzer task run proxy-config --output

Back to this machine alone: sudo morzer config unset listen.

Beyond 127.0.0.1 the password can't be turned off: an open proxy on a LAN serves whoever else gets on it.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Set one with sudo morzer config set <name>=<value>; edit a rules parameter with sudo morzer config edit <name>.

Name Default listen 127.0.0.1 the address the proxy port is published on; anything but 127.0.0.1 asks devices for proxy_user and proxy_password (sharing) port 7890 the SOCKS5 and HTTP proxy port proxy_user dotdash the username devices give beyond 127.0.0.1 direct_rules a comment destinations reached around dotdash, one rule per line (rules) block_rules a comment destinations refused, one rule per line subscription_interval 3600 seconds between fetches of the subscription probe_url https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204 what picking the fastest link and the health check fetch through dotdash gateway false under tun, this machine is its LAN's gateway, and doctor checks the host for it (gateway) dns_listen off under tun, the address and port that answers the LAN's DNS, such as 192.168.1.10:53

Profiles (installation.profile): tun, the whole machine.

items.title: Secrets
items.text: Name Generated subscription_url no the device's subscription URL, as the server's client-config prints it proxy_password yes the password devices give beyond 127.0.0.1

items.title: Tasks
items.text: Task proxy-config --output [-- <address>] the proxy URLs and credentials devices need; the address only with listen=0.0.0.0

items.title: Health
items.text: doctor and each apply fetch probe_url through dotdash, and with gateway=true check that the host forwards the LAN into TUN.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
Everything goes through dotdash unless a rule says otherwise. Two parameters hold the rules:

  • direct_rules: destinations reached directly, around dotdash;
  • block_rules: destinations refused.

Each is mihomo's classical rules without the target, one per line, with # for comments:

# around dotdash
DOMAIN-SUFFIX,example.ru
IP-CIDR,192.168.0.0/16,no-resolve

Edit them in an editor, or set them from a file:

sudo morzer config edit direct_rules
sudo morzer config set --set-file direct_rules=rules.txt

items.title: No resolving for IP rules
items.text: Give IP rules no-resolve. Without it, mihomo looks up every name on this machine's resolver to match them, which tells that resolver every name that goes through dotdash.

items.title: When dotdash is out of reach
items.text: With no links at all, as on a first start that can't fetch the subscription, everything but the direct rules is refused: nothing leaves around dotdash by accident.

items.title: The whole machine
items.text:
The tun profile sends every connection on the machine through dotdash, with no proxy settings: its Docker containers' and IPv6 included. The proxy port and the rules stay as they are.

sudo morzer config set installation.profile=tun
sudo morzer config unset installation.profile     # back to the proxy port alone
  • DNS answers with fake addresses, and the names go to dotdash, which resolves them. The machine's own resolver answers only for dotdash's server names and the direct rules.
  • With dotdash out of reach, nothing gets out around it.
  • Networks the machine is directly on, such as its LAN, stay reachable directly.
  • The subscription and the dotdash server must be reachable over the machine's main interface, as they normally are.

mihomo then runs as root with NET_ADMIN and DAC_OVERRIDE, on the host's network, with /dev/net/tun: a TUN interface takes nothing less. Its root filesystem stays read-only.

items.title: A gateway for the LAN
items.text:
Under tun, the machine can be its LAN's gateway: devices whose gateway is its address go through dotdash too, with nothing to set up on them.

It is a gateway beside the main router, on the same LAN: one network interface, and the main router keeps the internet link and hands out addresses. It doesn't replace the router. Making this machine the LAN's only router, with two interfaces, its own DHCP server and NAT, is host setup that dotdash leaves to you; a router system such as OpenWrt suits that better.

It carries IPv4 only. IPv6 from the LAN can't go through it, so step 4 turns IPv6 off around it, before any device is pointed at it.

Note

192.168.1.10 below stands for this machine's LAN address (hostname -I shows it): use yours.

  1. Turn it on, so doctor checks the host for it:

    sudo morzer config set gateway=true

  2. Let the host forward. It must forward IPv4:

    echo net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/90-dotdash-gateway.conf
sudo sysctl --system

    Docker sets the host's FORWARD policy to DROP on many machines, which drops the LAN's traffic before TUN sees it (dropped, never sent around dotdash). Two rules in Docker's DOCKER-USER chain let it through:

    sudo iptables -I DOCKER-USER -o Meta -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -I DOCKER-USER -i Meta -j ACCEPT

    They don't outlive a reboot by themselves: add them to whatever restores the host's firewall, or to a systemd unit that runs after docker.service. doctor names whichever is missing.

  3. Answer the LAN's DNS, if devices are to ask this machine:

    sudo morzer config set dns_listen=192.168.1.10:53

    Not 0.0.0.0:53, which clashes with systemd-resolved's stub.

  4. Turn IPv6 off around it. A main router that advertises IPv6 gives every device a second way out, straight past this machine. Turn off IPv6, or its router advertisements, on the main router; failing that, on each device. Then check on this machine:

    ip -6 route show default     # prints nothing once the main router stops advertising

    A line with proto ra there means the LAN still has IPv6 from the main router.

  5. Point devices at it: hand out 192.168.1.10 as the gateway (and DNS server) from the main router's DHCP, or set it on each device.

  6. Check from a device: an IP checker shows the dotdash exit, and an IPv6 test (curl -6 https://api6.ipify.org) fails rather than showing the device's own address.

items.title: Changelog
items.text:
All notable changes to this project are documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

items.title: Deprecated
items.text: • The xdns-xhttp-reality profile goes in 0.6.0, not in this patch release as 0.5.0 announced: removing it would break a server still set to it. xdns,xhttp-reality deploys the same; switch before 0.6.0 with sudo morzer config set installation.profile=xdns,xhttp-reality.

items.title: Fixed
items.text: • The command relay-config prints for the relay machine's last step, relay-entry, now includes --output; without it morzer ran the task and showed nothing, not the line the relays parameter needs.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Every bundle ships the key it is signed with, so morzer init needs no --signing-key: it prints the key, trusts it, and requires every later release to be signed by it. --signing-key still checks even the first release against the repository's.

  • A relay for networks that let only domestic addresses through: dotdash-relay, a new bundle released with dotdash, carries devices from a machine inside the country on to this server over port 443. The relay-config task prints its setup; its line in the new relays parameter adds a link through it for every device.

  • A client for a Linux machine or a network: dotdash-client, a new bundle released with dotdash, runs mihomo from one device's subscription URL, refreshed through dotdash, with a SOCKS5 and HTTP proxy port, block and direct rules, and a password once the port is published beyond the machine.

  • dotdash-client's tun profile sends every connection on the machine through dotdash with no proxy settings, its containers' and IPv6 included, with DNS answered by fake addresses whose names dotdash resolves; nothing gets out around dotdash when it is out of reach.

  • Under tun, dotdash-client can be its LAN's gateway: devices that use it as theirs go through dotdash too. gateway=true has doctor check that the host forwards the LAN into TUN, naming the two DOCKER-USER rules a FORWARD policy of DROP needs, and dns_listen answers the LAN's DNS.

  • mihomo connects over REALITY and XHTTP with REALITY: those links now carry support-x25519mlkem768=true, without which mihomo leaves out the key share Xray's REALITY requires and fails with "REALITY authentication failed". Other clients pass over the parameter.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• Every bundle of this release needs morzer 0.15.0: run sudo morzer self-update before updating. An older manager refuses the release and changes nothing.

  • The DNS tunnel and XHTTP with REALITY run together as installation.profile=xdns,xhttp-reality, two profiles combined.

  • upstream6 is no longer generated as a placeholder: a fresh install has none until the IPv6 proxy is turned on. An existing value is kept.

  • Unattended updates apply releases again, and morzer rollback works again, both of which 0.4.0 turned off for its own change of the upstream settings. An update from 0.3.x is still refused until the upstream secret is set.

  • bootstrap.sh is served from the documentation site: curl -fsSLO https://morzecrew.github.io/dotdash/bootstrap.sh. The documentation itself moved from the README to https://morzecrew.github.io/dotdash/, one version per release.

items.title: Deprecated
items.text: • The xdns-xhttp-reality profile: xdns,xhttp-reality deploys the same. It goes in the next release.

items.title: Fixed
items.text: • bootstrap.sh installs morzer 0.15.0, which the bundles require. It installed 0.13.0, so init on a freshly prepared host refused the release until morzer self-update.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• The upstream proxy is one secret, upstream, holding user:pass@host:port, so changing proxy is one restart; upstream_host, upstream_port, upstream_username and upstream_password no longer work. Run sudo morzer secret set upstream before updating: an update without it is refused.

  • This release is never applied unattended, and morzer rollback from it is refused, since 0.3.x could not start without the old settings; the pre-update backup is the way back.

  • The IPv6 proxy is the upstream6 secret in the same form, turned on by upstream6_protocol (socks or http, now none by default) instead of upstream6_host. With it on, set upstream6 and upstream6_protocol before updating, or IPv6 goes back to the first proxy.

  • Links are named after the device and transport, such as phone [reality], phone [xhttp] and phone [xhttp+reality], in place of dotdash-phone, dotdash-xhttp-phone and dotdash-xhttp-reality-phone. Apps show the new names once the links are added again, or at the next subscription refresh.

  • With subscriptions on, client-config prints each device's subscription URL alone, so the output stays short; --full before the device's name (-- --full phone) adds its links and Xray config, as before. With subscriptions off it prints what it always did.

  • The subscription service reports healthy only once every device's subscription is written: an apply or an update waits for it, and doctor names the service when that never happens.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Optional subscriptions (subscription): each device gets a URL on the cover site that serves its links, which client-config prints and the app refreshes by itself, so a revocation or a key rotation reaches devices without resending links. Rotating subscription_key moves every URL.

  • An optional second proxy for IPv6 (upstream6_host, with its own credentials), for an upstream that leaves over IPv4 only: destinations with an IPv6 address, sites with both included, leave through it, and the rest through the first. Neither falls back to the other, and doctor names the one that fails.

items.title: Changed
items.text: • The Xray config client-config prints checks all its entries at once every 30 seconds, where it checked one a minute in turn, so it leaves an entry that stops answering within about half a minute instead of up to several minutes. That is two small requests a minute per entry.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• The exit-check task prints the IPv4 and IPv6 addresses the upstream leaves from, each with its network and country, and says whether IPv6 is unavailable or leaves from another network than IPv4. It changes nothing.

  • Every apply and update, and every doctor, checks the release's invariants against what runs: traffic leaves through the upstream only, every inbound demands a client, and only the bundle's own ports are published, by unprivileged containers. An update that breaks one is rolled back; drift fails doctor.

  • An optional third transport: XHTTP under REALITY instead of TLS, on a port of its own (xhttp_reality_port, 8443). The xhttp-reality profile turns it on, xdns-xhttp-reality with the DNS tunnel; client-config then prints a third link and outbound, and the first two as before.

  • The canary's measure task fetches a URL through each transport N times and prints, as JSON, how many succeeded, timed out or failed, and the latency of those that succeeded.

  • The canary's xhttp-reality profile checks XHTTP with REALITY beside REALITY, on the server's xhttp_reality_port.

  • Both bundles carry signed build provenance, naming the commit and workflow run that built them. Check it with gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash:<version> --owner morzecrew, beside the signature morzer verifies.

  • With several servers (servers), canary-config also prints how to point a canary at each of the others: they share the secrets, so only server and address change.

  • The Xray config client-config prints answers the device's DNS, in an app's VPN or TUN mode, over DNS-over-HTTPS (dns_resolver) through the tunnel, with IPv4 addresses only: lookups no longer reach the local network's resolver or need the upstream to relay UDP. The README covers each app.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• Both bundles need morzer 0.14.0 or later. sudo morzer secret edit vless_clients then opens the list as plain text, one client per line, and init needs no --product.

  • When the way out fails, doctor says which layer did: the upstream proxy's address, its credentials, the destination behind it, or an exit that no longer matches healthcheck_expect. The health checks are now cover-site and egress.

  • Xray's log_level defaults to error. At warning and below it names the destinations of failed connections, which a log should not keep; set it back for debugging.

  • client-config prints one complete Xray config per device, for one server too: it uses whichever of REALITY and XHTTP answers fastest on any listed server, and the DNS tunnel only when none answers, instead of printing the tunnel's outbound alone.

items.title: Fixed
items.text:
• The cover site's error answers, such as 404 and 405, no longer name the server, and carry the site's headers like its pages do. A prober could tell them apart.

  • The canary's xhttp profile applies. Its Compose file found the base file by a path relative to a directory morzer does not run Compose from, so the profile failed validation.

  • A failed first apply, of dotdash or the canary, no longer leaves a directory where Xray's rendered configuration goes, which made every later apply fail to render it. A missing configuration file or Caddyfile now stops the container from starting instead.

items.title: Security
items.text:
• The upstream no longer learns which hostnames clients visit: this server resolves them over DNS-over-HTTPS sent through the upstream (resolve=gateway, the default) and hands it addresses only. A name resolving to a private address is blocked; resolve=upstream restores the old behaviour.

  • Xray has no route out of the machine. It runs on internal networks only, and a small gate container forwards the public port to it and carries its traffic to the upstream, whose credentials only the gate holds. Whatever Xray's own config says, it cannot send traffic past the upstream.

  • Caddy no longer writes the XHTTP path, a secret, to its log: it logs errors only, and never the request they concern, so no URI, header or client address either. An XHTTP session cut off mid-response used to log all three.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• A morzer bundle for one Docker host, published as ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash: releases as :X.Y.Z and :stable, signed with the release key, and every change to main as :main, signed with the dev key. Requires morzer 0.13.0, Docker 28 and Compose 2.35, or later.

  • REALITY on port 443: a client holding the key reaches Xray over VLESS with Vision, and anything else reaches a Caddy cover site with a Let's Encrypt certificate. https_port moves both to another host port.

  • XHTTP over TLS behind one secret path of the cover site, which also works through a CDN that proxies HTTP/2 to the server.

  • An optional DNS tunnel on UDP/53, VLESS over mKCP with XDNS, for networks where only DNS gets through. The xdns profile turns it on, at install or later; its zone is t.<domain> unless xdns_domain names another.

  • Every inbound uses VLESS Encryption (ML-KEM-768). morzer generates every key, short id and path at install, so no secret is chosen by hand.

  • All client traffic leaves through an upstream SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy you provide, optionally over TLS, with no direct fallback. UDP is relayed only through a SOCKS5 upstream that supports it (upstream_udp).

  • Xray is healthy only while it fetches a URL through the upstream, and doctor fails while it cannot. With healthcheck_expect, a response that does not match, such as a changed exit IP, fails it too.

  • An apply or update succeeds only once port 443 serves the cover site with a certificate a browser trusts.

  • The client-config task prints each device's REALITY and XHTTP links, and the DNS tunnel's outbound when it is on. With servers naming servers that share the keys, it prints links for each and an Xray config that uses whichever answers fastest.

  • One VLESS id per device in vless_clients: deleting a device's line revokes that device alone.

  • The cover site serves your own static files from site_dir wherever they have the requested path, and otherwise a bundled page titled with the server's domain.

  • cert_issuer=internal takes the certificate from Caddy's own CA instead of Let's Encrypt, for a machine the internet cannot reach.

  • Unattended updates: the bundle declares that it keeps no database and is safe to roll back, which morzer requires before it installs a release on its own. Nightly backups include Caddy's certificates.

  • The canary-config task prints the init command and secrets for a dotdash-canary machine acting as one of the clients.

  • dotdash-canary, a second bundle released with dotdash as ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-canary, for a machine inside a network you care about, such as a box at home. It connects to a dotdash server as an ordinary client and needs no open port.

  • The canary's health check fetches probe_url through dotdash over REALITY, and with the xhttp profile also over XHTTP, in up to three tries. doctor fails when all three fail, so a notify target at its default level hears that the network lost its way out.

  • Services run as a non-root user in read-only containers with every capability dropped. Xray's access log is always off.

  • scripts/bootstrap.sh prepares a fresh Debian or Ubuntu server: Docker, sops, age and morzer, unattended security updates, and SSH with keys only once an authorized key exists.

items.title: Releases and CI
items.text:
bundle-ci builds, signs and smoke-tests every pull request and push. A push to main publishes :main; a vX.Y.Z tag publishes all four bundles as :X.Y.Z and :stable, with a GitHub release. Each bundle carries signed build provenance:

gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash:<version> --owner morzecrew

A weekly benchmark measures REALITY and XHTTP under added latency and loss; it informs and never gates. Check a bundle change with morzer release verify ./bundle --render-check.

items.title: Documentation
items.text:
This site is Zensical with mike versions on the gh-pages branch. A push to main that touches pages/ publishes dev; a vX.Y.Z tag publishes X.Y and, for the newest minor, moves latest and the root to it.

cd pages && uv run zensical serve    # http://localhost:8047

The diagrams are d2 sources in pages/diagrams, rendered once for the light scheme and once for the dark one into pages/docs/assets/diagrams. The build doesn't run d2: after changing a .d2 file, run pages/diagrams/render.sh and commit the SVGs.

items.title: Relay
items.text: Some networks inside the country let only domestic addresses through: mobile networks do this during shutdowns, with an allowlist. A device there can't reach a dotdash server abroad at all. The dotdash-relay bundle (ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-relay) runs on a machine inside the country, whose address does get through, and carries devices on to the server.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
• Devices connect to the relay on 443 with REALITY, under the name of a site next to it: its site parameter, a real site in the relay's own network. To the network, the connection looks like one to that site.
  • Anyone probing the relay's 443 gets that site's real TLS handshake.
  • The relay has keys of its own, and its own copy of the devices allowed in. A device uses the same id as on the server, with a separate link per relay, phone [relay <host>].
  • The relay goes on to the server as one client of its own, a line in the server's vless_clients. With several servers, it uses whichever answers fastest, so a ban on one address doesn't cut it off.
  • Nothing leaves the relay except to dotdash: traffic still exits through the server's upstream proxy.

It can also help where home and mobile lines slow down TLS to foreign hosting: devices then reach only a domestic address, and the relay's own link to the server runs from its hosting network, which the slowdown may not reach.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• The relay's address must get through. Whether one does depends on the network, the provider and the day. Test it from a SIM on such a network before relying on it.
  • On those networks only 443 and TCP get through: the DNS tunnel is no use there.
  • Devices need the relay links before a shutdown. An app can't refresh a subscription from the server's site while only domestic addresses get through.
  • The machine needs Docker, sops, age and morzer (bootstrap.sh), and port 443 free.
  • The official sing-box apps, Karing and NekoBox can't connect to dotdash, relay or not: they lack VLESS Encryption and the key share Xray's REALITY requires.

Next: set one up.

items.title: Set up a relay
items.text: Setting up a relay moves between three places: the dotdash server, the relay machine, and back. The server prints everything the relay needs, and the relay prints the one line the server needs back:

items.title: 1. Pick the site
items.text:
The relay borrows the name of a site next to it: devices send that name, and probes get that site's handshake. Pick one that is:

  • in the relay's own network, the same hosting provider or nearby, not a big name served from somewhere else;

  • on TLS 1.3 and HTTP/2. curl prints 2 for one that is, and fails for one without TLS 1.3:

    curl -so /dev/null --tlsv1.3 --http2 -w '%{http_version}\n' https://site.example.ru

items.title: 2. On the server: a client for the relay
items.text:
Add a <uuid> relay line to vless_clients (uuidgen makes an id), then print the relay's setup:

sudo EDITOR=nano morzer secret edit vless_clients
sudo morzer task run relay-config --output -- relay

The output is every device's credentials

It carries the relay's copy of vless_clients. Move it to the relay machine as you would a password.

items.title: 3. On the relay: install
items.text:
Install Docker, sops, age and morzer (bootstrap.sh), and make a recovery key as for the server:

morzer secret recipients generate-recovery-key ~/relay-recovery.key   # keep it off the machine

Then run what step 2 printed, with your site and the recovery key's age1… filled in. It has this shape:

sudo morzer init --release oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-relay:stable \
  --recovery-recipient age1… \
  --set site=site.example.ru \
  --set dotdash_servers=example.com --set dotdash_port=443 \
  --set dotdash_public_key=…
sudo morzer secret set dotdash_id <<'END'          # and dotdash_encryption,
…                                                  # dotdash_short_id,
END                                                # vless_clients
sudo morzer apply

apply succeeds once the relay gets out through dotdash. The relay generates its own keys at init.

items.title: 4. On the relay: its line
items.text:
Give relay-entry the address devices reach the relay at, its public IP or a name pointing at it:

sudo morzer task run relay-entry --output -- 198.51.100.7

It prints one line for the server, its own address, site, public key, short id and encryption, plus the commands a canary needs to check this relay:

198.51.100.7 site.example.ru <public key> <short id> <encryption>

items.title: 5. On the server: add the line to relays
items.text:
One line per relay:

sudo morzer config edit relays

items.title: 6. Devices
items.text:
client-config now prints a [relay 198.51.100.7] link for every device, and the Xray config falls back to the relays when the server itself is out of reach. Subscriptions pick the link up by themselves; otherwise resend the links. Do it now, while devices can still reach the server.

To check, connect a phone on the target network with its relay link alone.

Next: keeping it running.

items.title: Running a relay
items.text: The relay keeps copies of what it got from the server: the devices, and the server's keys. Whatever changes one side has to reach the other.

items.title: Devices
items.text:
A device added to or deleted from the server's vless_clients has to change on the relay too. After the change on the server, relay-config prints the relay's new copy:

# on the server
sudo morzer task run relay-config --output -- relay
# on the relay: the vless_clients block of that output
sudo morzer secret set vless_clients <<'END'
…
END

items.title: Keys
items.text: What changed What to do The server's reality_key, vless_seed or reality_short_id Run relay-config again, and on the relay set dotdash_public_key, dotdash_encryption and dotdash_short_id from it. Until then the relay can't reach the server. The relay's own keys (secret rotate on the relay) Run relay-entry again, replace the relay's line in the server's relays, and send devices their links again (subscriptions pick them up). The relay's address The same: relay-entry -- <new address>, then replace the line.

items.title: Servers
items.text:
The relay goes to every server in dotdash_servers and uses whichever answers fastest. With a new server sharing the keys:

sudo morzer config set dotdash_servers=example.com,b.example.com

items.title: Watching it
items.text:
doctor and each apply fetch probe_url through dotdash, so they fail when the relay can't reach the server. Have them alert you:

sudo morzer notify target add https://hooks.example/morzer

What the relay can't see is whether devices reach it: only a machine on the networks devices use can. A canary there checks the relay as it checks a server, with the commands relay-entry prints.

items.title: Updates
items.text: As for the server: sudo morzer self-update when a release needs a newer morzer, then sudo morzer update --stage && sudo morzer update --to <version>. Unattended updates follow update.channel=oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-relay:stable; see Operations.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Set one with sudo morzer config set <name>=<value>.

Name Default site none, given at init a site next to the relay, in its own network, on TLS 1.3 and HTTP/2: devices send its name, and probes get its handshake dotdash_servers none, given at init the dotdash servers sharing one set of keys, comma-separated domains; the relay uses whichever answers fastest dotdash_port 443 the servers' https_port dotdash_public_key none, given at init the servers' REALITY public key, the pbk of their links dotdash_address none where to connect when dotdash_servers names one server, such as its IP; none reaches each server by its name probe_url https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204 what the health check fetches through dotdash; any 2xx is healthy dotdash_server none deprecated: the one server, read only while dotdash_servers is unset

items.title: Secrets
items.text:
init generates the relay's own keys; the rest come from the server's relay-config.

Name Generated vless_clients no the devices the relay lets in, one <uuid> [name] per line dotdash_id no the id the relay uses on the server, its line in the server's vless_clients dotdash_encryption no the encryption= value of the server's links dotdash_short_id no the sid= value of the server's REALITY links vless_seed yes the seed the relay's VLESS Encryption key pair derives from reality_key yes the relay's REALITY private key reality_short_id yes the relay's REALITY short id

items.title: Tasks
items.text: Task relay-entry --output -- <address> the relay's line for the server's relays, and how a canary checks the relay

items.title: Server
items.text:
The dotdash bundle (ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash) runs on one Docker host outside the censored network. Devices connect to it on 443, and it sends their traffic on through your upstream proxy, the only way out it has.

  • gate is the only container with a route out. It forwards the public ports in to Xray and carries Xray's traffic out to the upstream proxy, whose credentials only it holds.
  • Xray answers on 443 with REALITY. A dotdash device goes on through the upstream; anything else, a censor's probe or a browser, is handed to Caddy, so 443 looks like an ordinary HTTPS site.
  • Caddy serves that site with a trusted certificate, each device's subscription URL, and XHTTP on a secret path, which is what lets XHTTP pass through a CDN.

The upstream is a SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy you choose, typically one with a residential exit. With it down, devices get nothing, never the server's own address: what leaks where.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Install the server.
  2. Connect devices: links, an Xray config, or subscriptions.
  3. Optional:
  4. your own cover site;
  5. a DNS tunnel for networks that pass little but DNS;
  6. XHTTP with REALITY on another port;
  7. a second proxy for IPv6;
  8. a CDN in front of XHTTP;
  9. several servers sharing one set of keys.
  10. Operations: updates, alerts, backups, and moving to a new server.

items.title: CDN
items.text: The XHTTP link works through a CDN that proxies HTTP/2 to https://example.com: put the CDN's name in the link's address. Check its terms first; Cloudflare's self-serve plans forbid proxies.

items.title: ECH through Cloudflare
items.text:
ECH also hides example.com from the network: the TLS handshake then shows cloudflare-ech.com. Cloudflare turns ECH on by default. Add it to the XHTTP link, before the # (v2rayN ≥ 7.17, v2rayNG ≥ 2.0):

&ech=cloudflare-ech.com%2Bhttps%3A%2F%2F1.1.1.1%2Fdns-query

In the Xray config, add the same to that outbound's tlsSettings:

"echConfigList": "cloudflare-ech.com+https://1.1.1.1/dns-query"

With ECH set, the connection fails rather than falling back to plain SNI.

items.title: Cover site
items.text:
Anyone who opens https://example.com, or probes 443, gets the cover site. The bundled page differs between servers only in its title, so one server seen reveals the others. Give each its own: static files in /srv/dotdash (the site_dir parameter), readable by uid 65532. Caddy serves them as they change, with no restart, and falls back to the bundled page for a file that isn't there.

sudo mkdir -p /srv/dotdash
sudo cp -r ./my-site/. /srv/dotdash/
sudo chmod -R a+rX /srv/dotdash

items.title: DNS on devices
items.text:
The Xray config from client-config answers port-53 DNS over DoH through the tunnel, IPv4 only, and fails rather than asking the local network. Links leave DNS to the app. As of November 2026:

  • v2rayNG: import as a custom config, and keep the SOCKS port at 10808.
  • v2rayN: TUN with a custom config needs the profile's "Socks port" at
  • DNS then follows v2rayN's settings, so keep them on the proxy.
  • Hiddify drops a config's DNS and routing: use the links. Its own DNS goes through the proxy by default.
  • iOS: Happ runs the config; set "Tunnel DNS" and "Include all networks". Check Streisand and V2Box on a DNS leak test site.

items.title: Devices
items.text:
Each device has its own id, a <uuid> [name] line in the vless_clients secret. init creates the first; add one per device:

uuidgen                                          # a new id
sudo EDITOR=nano morzer secret edit vless_clients  # add "<uuid> phone"; Xray restarts on save

items.title: Links and the Xray config
items.text:
sudo morzer task run client-config --output             # every device
sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- phone    # one

Per device it prints:

  • a REALITY link and an XHTTP link, phone [reality] and phone [xhttp], for each server; phone [xhttp+reality] with XHTTP with REALITY on; and phone [relay <host>] for each relay;
  • an Xray config for v2rayN or v2rayNG (as a custom config) that uses whichever link answers fastest, drops a dead one within about 30 s, and falls back to the DNS tunnel when it is on.

The output is a password

Anyone holding a device's links can use the server as that device.

As QR codes in the terminal, with qrencode:

sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- phone | grep '^vless://' |
  while read -r link; do qrencode -t ansiutf8 "$link"; done

How each app handles DNS: DNS on devices.

items.title: Subscriptions
items.text:
With subscriptions on, each device gets one URL instead, and fetches its links from it:

sudo morzer config set subscription=true
sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- phone           # its URL only
sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- --full phone    # plus links and the Xray config
  • Add the URL as a subscription in the app (v2rayN, v2rayNG, Hiddify, Happ, Streisand) and refresh every few hours: revocations, key rotations and new relays then reach devices with nothing to resend.
  • mihomo reads the URL as an http proxy provider; the client bundle runs it on a Linux machine for you.
  • A URL is as secret as the links. sudo morzer secret rotate subscription_key moves every URL; any other path gets the site's 404.

The official sing-box apps, Karing and NekoBox can't connect to dotdash: they lack VLESS Encryption and the key share Xray's REALITY requires.

items.title: Revoking a device
items.text:
Delete its line from vless_clients. A revoked device still knows the shared keys; to hide the server from it too, rotate them and resend links (subscriptions pick them up):

sudo morzer secret rotate reality_key
sudo morzer secret rotate vless_seed

With relays or several servers, change their copies too.

items.title: DNS tunnel
items.text:
A fallback for networks that pass little but DNS. The Xray config from client-config switches to it when the other transports fail.

ns.example.com.  A   <server IP>
t.example.com.   NS  ns.example.com.

Open 53/udp, then add --profile xdns to init, or:

sudo morzer config set installation.profile=xdns

If systemd-resolved holds port 53, set xdns_bind to the public IP.

items.title: A domain of its own
items.text:
Better: a resolver that flags tunnel queries blocks the domain above them, which would take the site with it. Use a cheap, unrelated domain (example.net) for nothing but the tunnel:

; at example.net's DNS provider
ns.example.net.  A   <server IP>
t.example.net.   NS  ns.example.net.

dig +short NS t.example.net                       # ns.example.net. once delegated
sudo morzer config set xdns_domain=t.example.net
sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- --full phone   # resend: the config names the zone

items.title: Install
items.text:
You need a domain, a Linux host abroad, and an upstream proxy. example.com stands for your domain throughout.

  1. DNS: point the domain at the server:

    example.com.  A  <server IP>

  2. Firewall: open 80/tcp and 443/tcp in the cloud provider's firewall (on Google Cloud, a VPC firewall rule). Docker's published ports bypass ufw and firewalld, so the provider's firewall is the one that counts. Allow SSH with keys only.

  3. Host: install Docker, sops, age and morzer, with bootstrap.sh on Debian or Ubuntu.

  4. Recovery key: it decrypts the backups. Make it, and keep it off the machine:

    morzer secret recipients generate-recovery-key ~/dotdash-recovery.key

    It prints the public half, age1…, which the next step takes.

  5. Deploy:

    sudo morzer init --release oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash:stable \
  --domain example.com --recovery-recipient age1…
sudo morzer secret set upstream    # user:pass@host:port
sudo morzer apply
    • Add --set upstream_protocol=http for an HTTP proxy, and --set upstream_tls=true if it takes TLS. The default is SOCKS5.
    • upstream is user:pass@host:port, or host:port with no login. The password may contain : and @; an IPv6 host goes in brackets; no socks5:// prefix. Changing proxy later is one secret set and one restart.
    • init prints the release's signing key and trusts it. To check even this first release against the key published with the repository, add --signing-key "$(gh variable get MINISIGN_RELEASE_PUBKEY -R morzecrew/dotdash)".

  6. Check: apply succeeds only once Xray reaches the internet through the upstream and 443 serves the site with a trusted certificate. Later, at any time:

    sudo morzer doctor                        # health, and the failing layer if any
sudo morzer task run exit-check --output  # the exit sites see

Next: connect devices.

items.title: IPv6 through a second proxy
items.text:
For an IPv4-only upstream: destinations with an IPv6 address, dual-stack ones included, leave through the IPv6 proxy, the rest through the first. Neither falls back to the other.

sudo morzer secret set upstream6                  # user:pass@host:port, first
sudo morzer config set upstream6_protocol=socks   # or http; upstream6_tls=true if needed
sudo morzer task run exit-check --output

Needs resolve=gateway (the default). Two providers show as MISMATCH in exit-check, as expected. Off: sudo morzer config unset upstream6_protocol.

items.title: What leaks where
items.text:
• Traffic leaves only through the upstream. With the upstream down, clients get nothing, never this server's address. Xray has no route out; a gate container holds the upstream's credentials. Every apply, update and doctor checks this against what runs.
  • The upstream sees destination addresses, ports and volume, not hostnames: this server resolves them over DoH (dns_resolver), through the upstream. SNI stays visible unless the client uses ECH. resolve=upstream hands the upstream the hostnames.
  • On the device, only the app keeps traffic inside a dropped tunnel (TUN with a kill switch, or Android's "block connections without VPN"). A browser IP checker showing an IPv6 address that exit-check calls unavailable sees the device's own: route IPv6 into the tunnel or turn it off in the app.

items.title: Moving to a new server
items.text:
Prepare: keep the recovery key off the machine, add a backup target, and set the A record's TTL to 300 s or less. Devices keep their links.

# on the new server, after bootstrap.sh
sudo morzer --product dotdash installation import --from-backup \
  --target s3://bucket/dotdash --credentials-file ./bucket.yaml \
  --identity ~/dotdash-recovery.key
sudo morzer update oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash:stable
# optional, keeps Caddy's certificate (import prints both ids)
sudo morzer backup fetch <backup id>
sudo morzer restore --force --confirm <installation id> --identity ~/dotdash-recovery.key

Then point example.com (and ns.example.com) at the new IP and shut the old machine down: two live servers with one installation id confuse each other's backups.

items.title: Operations
items.text:
Updates, alerts, backups and doctor work the same on relay, client and canary machines; only the update channel names another bundle.

Task Command Update by hand sudo morzer update --stage && sudo morzer update --to <version> New morzer sudo morzer self-update Backups off the machine sudo morzer backup target add s3://bucket/dotdash --credentials backup_s3 Alerts sudo morzer notify target add https://hooks.example/morzer Health and faults sudo morzer doctor Which exit sites see sudo morzer task run exit-check --output Metrics for Prometheus sudo morzer config set metrics.textfile=/var/lib/prometheus/node-exporter

items.title: Unattended updates
items.text:
From :stable, nightly at 03:30.

Warning

This gives whoever holds the release key root on the machine.

sudo morzer config set update.check=true
sudo morzer config set update.channel=oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash:stable
sudo morzer config set update.auto_apply=true

items.title: Pin the exit IP
items.text:
doctor fails when the provider moves you:

sudo morzer config set healthcheck_url=https://api.ipify.org 'healthcheck_expect=^203\.0\.113\.7\s*$'

items.title: What the checks say
items.text:
• Alerts cover failed applies, updates and backups, and each morning's doctor, which names the failing layer: the proxy's address, its credentials, the destination, or the exit.
  • exit-check: "IPv6 unavailable" means the upstream has no IPv6 exit, which is not a leak. "MISMATCH" means IPv4 and IPv6 leave from different networks.
  • Backups run nightly: secrets, encrypted to the recovery key, and Caddy's certificates. See morzer's operating docs.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Name Default upstream_protocol socks socks or http; the proxy is the upstream secret upstream_tls false TLS to the upstream upstream_udp false relay UDP via a SOCKS5 upstream with UDP ASSOCIATE; otherwise dropped upstream6_protocol none socks or http turns on the IPv6 proxy, the upstream6 secret upstream6_tls false TLS to the IPv6 proxy https_port 443 host port for REALITY and the site xdns_domain t tunnel zone (xdns); a name with no dot is under the domain xdns_bind 0.0.0.0 host address for UDP/53 xdns_mtu 900 tunnel reply size; lower it if replies get lost xhttp_reality_port 8443 port for XHTTP with REALITY; not https_port or 80 log_level error Xray error log; warning and below name failed destinations healthcheck_url https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204 fetched through the upstream healthcheck_expect .* regex the response must match, such as the exit IP healthcheck6_url http://api6.ipify.org IPv6-only URL fetched through the IPv6 proxy resolve gateway gateway: this server resolves over dns_resolver; upstream: the upstream sees hostnames dns_resolver https://1.1.1.1/dns-query DoH server for resolve=gateway and device DNS; https:// only subscription false a subscription URL per device cert_issuer acme acme (Let's Encrypt) or internal (offline machines) site_dir /srv/dotdash your own cover site servers self servers sharing these keys, comma-separated relays a comment one <host> <site> <public key> <short id> <encryption> line per relay, as its relay-entry prints it

Set one with sudo morzer config set <name>=<value>, unset it with sudo morzer config unset <name>, edit relays with sudo morzer config edit relays. Profiles (installation.profile): xdns, xhttp-reality, or both as xdns,xhttp-reality; xdns-xhttp-reality does the same and goes in 0.6.0.

items.title: Secrets
items.text:
init generates every secret except upstream and upstream6. Set one with sudo morzer secret set <name>, edit with sudo morzer secret edit <name>, replace a generated one with sudo morzer secret rotate <name>.

Name Generated upstream no the upstream proxy, user:pass@host:port or host:port upstream6 no the IPv6 proxy, same form; needed once upstream6_protocol is set vless_clients yes one <uuid> [name] line per device vless_seed yes ML-KEM-768 seed the VLESS Encryption key pair derives from reality_key yes REALITY private key (x25519) reality_short_id yes REALITY short id clients present alongside the key xhttp_path yes secret path Caddy routes to Xray's XHTTP inbound subscription_key yes key the subscription URLs derive from

Rotating vless_seed, reality_key, reality_short_id or xhttp_path changes every link: resend them, or let subscriptions pick it up.

items.title: Several servers
items.text:
Same keys on every server, each under its own domain and the same https_port. Links then cover every server, and the Xray config fails over between them. Add and revoke devices on each.

# on the first server; sudo on b.example.com must not prompt
for s in vless_clients vless_seed reality_key reality_short_id xhttp_path; do
  sudo cat /run/dotdash/secrets/$s | ssh b.example.com sudo morzer secret set $s
done
# on every server
sudo morzer config set servers=example.com,b.example.com

items.title: XHTTP with REALITY
items.text:
A third link on its own port (xhttp_reality_port, 8443), for a network that passes another port better than 443. Xray-core clients (v2rayN, v2rayNG) and mihomo. Open the port in the provider's firewall, then:

sudo morzer config set installation.profile=xhttp-reality   # with the DNS tunnel: xdns,xhttp-reality

Off: set the previous profile (xdns) or sudo morzer config unset installation.profile, before any rollback to a release without it.
